title: The hidden partner
hook: showing off is called a hidden shirk, doing good for people's eyes (Ahmad)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tawhid, oneness from three sides, and your line: one in every way. Which side did the day touch for you? Today, a partner that sneaks in unnoticed. Day one thousand seventy.

A man stands to pray alone. His prayer is ordinary, a little quick. Then he notices someone has come into the room and is watching. His back straightens. His recitation slows and grows careful. Every movement becomes more beautiful. Nothing has changed except the audience. A report in the collection of Ibn Majah uses exactly that picture, and calls it a hidden shirk. Shirk means giving God a partner. Nobody in that room set up an idol. So where's the partner? Look at who the prayer is suddenly for.

Riya'. Showing off. Doing good for people's eyes. This whole week the shahadah has cleared the room: no god, but Allah. Riya' is how something slips back in through the side door. First, what the hadith calls it. In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, the Prophet tells his companions that what he fears for them is the lesser shirk. They ask what that is. He says: riya'. Not a statue. An audience. The deed still looks like worship, but part of it is quietly offered to the people watching. Second, the Qur'an names it too. Surah one hundred seven, in Pickthall's translation, warns of worshippers "Who would be seen (at worship)." And the end of surah eighteen asks the one who hopes to meet his Lord to "make none sharer of the worship due unto his Lord." Sharer, partner. Third, the answer the tradition gives is hiddenness. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes, among those shaded by God on a day with no other shade, a person who gave charity so secretly that his left hand didn't know what his right hand gave. Fourth, a balance, so this doesn't turn into fear. Sahih Muslim records the Prophet being asked about a man who does good and people praise him for it. He called it the early good news of the believer. Being seen isn't the problem. Doing it to be seen is. And some teachers warn against the opposite trap too: giving up a good deed for fear of what people will think lets the audience run your life all the same.

The practice: one good deed nobody will see. Settle, and breathe. Let ideas come. Paying for something quietly. Fixing what someone else left broken. Praying for a person who will never know you did. A kind word about someone who isn't in the room. Pick one you can actually do today, and plan it so no one finds out, not even with a hint later. Notice any small itch to tell. Let it pass, like a breath. If you pray, you can make the intention for God alone. The bell holds the time.
Riya'. Showing off: good done for people's eyes, the partner hidden inside a good deed. Today's word.
Your line: only for him. Today, do your unseen deed, and keep it unseen. Tomorrow, the Shia adhan. Day one thousand seventy.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to check their intention before a good deed, and hadith praise giving charity in secret, while some teachers also warn against abandoning good deeds out of fear of being seen.

fork.setup: you're about to do a good deed and you worry someone will see and you'll start doing it for them. what do the teachers say?
options: skip the deed, to be safe.
do it, and keep your intention for God.
do it only when a crowd is watching.
fork.reveal: giving up a good deed because of people is still letting people decide; the remedy is the intention, not the silence.

Index cites Ahmad for 'hidden shirk'; the Musnad Ahmad hadith (Mahmud ibn Labid) calls riya' 'the lesser shirk' and the hidden-shirk picture of beautifying one's prayer is from Ibn Majah 4204 (also reported elsewhere). The script attributes each to its collection; confirm numbers and that Ahmad's hadith begins 'what I fear most for you', paraphrased here as 'what he fears for them'.
Bukhari 1423 and Muslim 2642 numbers cited from memory; confirm.
'Some teachers warn against... giving up a good deed for fear of what people will think' echoes a saying commonly attributed to al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad; not attributed in the voice. Keeper may name him.
The surah numbers 'one hundred seven' and 'eighteen' are spoken as references; editor may prefer dropping them.
